questions.q: What UID does a container process run as if the Dockerfile never specifies a USER?
options: A randomly generated unprivileged UID chosen by the Docker daemon
The same UID as the user who ran docker build
Root (UID 0)
Containers cannot start at all without an explicit USER line
questions.explain: Without a USER instruction, the containerized process defaults to running as root (UID 0), which is convenient in development but unnecessary privilege in production.

questions.q: In `RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app -d /app -s /sbin/nologin app` followed later by `USER app`, what does the USER line change?
options: It switches the process UID for every subsequent instruction, including the final CMD/ENTRYPOINT, so the application runs unprivileged
It only affects the docker build process, not the running container
It deletes the root user from the image entirely
It has no effect unless paired with --read-only
questions.explain: USER switches which UID every following instruction, and critically the final CMD/ENTRYPOINT, executes as — this is the line that actually drops the running app to unprivileged.

questions.q: What does mounting a container with --read-only --tmpfs /tmp accomplish?
options: It prevents the container from starting unless it is run as root
It makes the root filesystem unwritable except for an explicit in-memory scratch mount, blocking an attacker from modifying application files or persisting changes
It disables networking for the container
It automatically drops all Linux capabilities as a side effect
questions.explain: --read-only locks the root filesystem against writes; --tmpfs /tmp supplies a small writable in-memory scratch space for the few things that genuinely need to write somewhere.

questions.q: What does `--cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE` do that simply not running as root does not?
options: It grants the container full root capabilities regardless of the USER instruction
It is purely cosmetic and has no runtime effect
It automatically scans the image for CVEs before granting capabilities
It narrows the process down to one specific Linux capability instead of the full bundle root implies, so even a compromised process has almost nothing extra it's allowed to do
questions.explain: Root bundles many discrete capabilities together; dropping all of them and re-adding only what's needed (like binding a privileged port) narrows what a compromised process can actually do.

questions.q: What does `runAsNonRoot: true` in a Kubernetes Pod's securityContext actually do?
options: It silently switches the container to run as root if the image would otherwise fail
It makes the kubelet refuse to start the pod at all if the image would run as root, turning a Dockerfile mistake into a deployment-time failure
It automatically rewrites the Dockerfile to add a USER instruction
It only applies a warning label in the Kubernetes dashboard with no enforcement
questions.explain: runAsNonRoot: true is enforced at pod startup — if the image's effective user would be root, the kubelet refuses to run it, catching the problem before it reaches production.
